Died at his parents' home after medical discharge on 31 December 1917. According to MÍH, he was bedridden for the last 9 weeks of his life, and in serious pain, but showed great endurance.

person.note: Regimental number 1084206. His parents were Guðmundur Magnússon Borgfjörð and Þórunn Hallgrímsdóttir of Arborg. Two older brothers, Magnús and Þorsteinn, also fought in the army. ("Alexander var hinn gerfilegasti í sjón og hið mesta mannsefni, og röskur til hvers er vera skyldi. Hann var fríðleiksmaður og drengskaparmaður í hvívetna.")

event.p: Enlisted in February 1916.

According to MÍH (with additional information from his service records), he was hit by a shell on 5 April 1917 at Neuville-St.-Vaast in France that mangled his right arm and left him with multiple serious wounds. Three days later, he arrived in hospital in France, on Easter Sunday, and three weeks later he was sent to England. His right arm was amputated at the shoulder. He spent the remaining few weeks of his life in hospital in England, at Stepping Hill and finally at Ramsgate. His wounds appeared to have completely healed when he succumbed to sepsis (tetanus according to his medical records; shrapnel had remained in his body).
Died at Princess Patricia's Canadian Red Cross Hospital in Ramsgate, Kent, England.

person.note: Regimental number 721948. His parents were Elízabet Gísladóttir (daughter of Gísli Eiríksson and Elízabet Jónsdóttir from Kríthóll in Skagjafjörður, Iceland) and Ágúst G. Archibald grew up with his parents: in Winnipeg to the age of 6, and later in Gimli, Manitoba. He went to school in Gimli, quitting in secondary school to begin working. He worked at various jobs, mainly as a store clerk. According to MÍH, he boarded a ship for England on 18 September 1916 and was on the front lines in France, from February to April 1917 at Vimy Ridge.

person.note: Regimental number 874097. His parents were bookseller Finnur Jónsson of Winnipeg and his wife Guðrún Ásgeirsdóttir. His father's family came from Melar in Hrútafjörður, where they had lived for nearly 300 years. His mother's family was from Mýrasýsla. Ásgeir's siblings were Anna (married to John P. Duncan, Antler, Saskatchewan) and Jón Ragnar (a student at the University of Manitoba at the time of MÍH's publication). According to MÍH, Ásgeir embarked for England in October 1916. He had grown up with his parents in Winnipeg and was described "by a man who knew him well" as a promising student, industrious and always reading. Gentle and sensitive by nature, very calm and collected, careful with his words and affectionate. He was a man of a good average height, burly, stood up straight and carried himself well. He was handsome, with a clear and kind expression, yet bold. ("Svo er honum lýst af manni, er þekti hann vel: 'Hann hafði farsælar námsgáfur, iðjusamur og sílesandi. Þýður og viðkvæmur í lundi, geðprúður í bezta lagi, orðvar og ástúðlegur í viðmóti. Hann var röskur meðalmaður að hæð, þrekinn, beinvaxinn og bar sig vel. Honum var vel farið í sjón, svipurinn hreinn og góðlegur, en þó djarflegur.")

On 13 August 1916 he fell suddenly ill at his home in Arborg and was brought to Winnipeg the same day for an operation. He did not recover and died in hospital a few days later.

person.note: His parents were Þorbergur Fjeldsted from Hvítárvellir in Borgarfjarðarsýsla and Helga Guðmundsdóttir from Hamraendir in Stafholtstungnahreppur (who died a year after arrival to Canada). The family moved to Winnipeg and from there to Hecla Island. Ásgeir worked in a store from an early age and worked for Sigurðsson-Thorvaldson in Arborg as the store manager from 1910. He married Ingunn Kristjónsdóttir Finnsson around this time. They had three boys. He was also survived by six siblings and three half-sisters. He was buried in Arborg Cemetery. According to MÍH, he loved music and he was handsome, with a dark complexion, well-built, excitable and talented in many fields. ("Ásgeir var friður sýnum, dökkur yfirlitum, liðlega vaxinn, ör í skapi og fjölhæfur á marga lundi. Hneigðist hugur hans að sönglist og hljómleikum.")

person.note: Regimental number 913510. His parents were Kristján S. Guðmundsson (d. 16 September 1918) and Helga Jóhanna Þórðardóttir, who emigrated in 1887 or 1888 from Ytri-Tunga in Tjörnes in Þingeyjarsýsla and settled near Gimli in New Iceland, Manitoba, Canada. Their other children were: the Rev. Albert Edvard of Lundar, Manitoba; Kristjana and María, both married; Sigtryggur; the merchant Hannes in Gimli; and Hallfríður. Baldur was a good athlete and loved music. According to MÍH, Baldur enlisted in the brass band of the 197th regiment on the condition that he not be required to bear arms. He was the band conductor for a time. But when the regiment arrived in England and the men assigned to new regiments, this agreement was not respected, and he was required to attend target practice even when he protested. However, from letters home to his family, his attitude towards the war appears to have been transformed after seeing the situation in England, and he now believed that it would be necessary for as many as possible to take up arms. He went to England in 1916 and that same winter to France. After some time in the trenches, he was given the opportunity of taking his old position (in the band) but refused the offer.

A good son to his mother, caring greatly for her well-being. He was survived by two full siblings and five half-siblings, two of whom lived in Iceland.

person.note: Regimental number 763406. His parents were Richard Shortt (Canadian, born in Arthur, Ontario) and his wife Aðalbjörg Einarsdóttir (whose father, Einar, was the farmer at Hóll í Kinn in Ljósavatnshreppur in Suður-Þingeyjarsýsla and emigrated to Canada in 1878), who lived in Cardwell. Stanley lived with his parents and worked mainly in the lumber industry prior to enlisting. According to MÍH, Stanley left for England with his regiment in April 1917. On arrival, most of the recruits in his battalion were assigned to the Forestry Corps, but according to MÍH, Stanley had not wanted to do forestry and roadwork and instead had chosen to leave for France with the machine gunners of the 116th Battalion. He fought at Lens, Merricourt, Loos and Amiens; he fell at the Battle of Amiens. Stanley is described as strong, hardy and energetic, and the best of men. ("vaskleikamaður, hraustur og þrekmikill og hinn bezti drengur.")

person.note: Regimental number 234090. His parents were Stefán Bjarnason from Naustahvammur and Guðbjörg Matthíasdóttir Long (granddaughter of Richard Long of England). When Einar was five, he was fostered by the Rev. Jón Guðmundsson from Nes in Norðfjörður, Iceland. Einar grew up with the family at Nes, and his foster-father paid for him to go to Reykjavík and learn to be a tailor. In the summer of 1909, Einar emigrated and headed for the Quill Lakes Settlement in Saskatchewan (Vatnabyggð). Einar adopted the Long family name on arrival to North America. Einar worked and studied in Saskatchewan before enrolling in the preparatory school of Wesley College in Winnipeg in the fall of 1911. His poor English skills were initially a hindrance to his studies, but one he quickly overcame. The most difficult challenge was his own poverty; he was helped to some degree by several people he had met. He was an arts student at Wesley College at the time he enlisted. In the last years of his studies, he had become increasingly involved in church matters and had held sermons at several Icelandic settlements. Over the winter, he held Sunday sermons for the Skjaldborg congregation in Winnipeg. He had decided to study theology and become a minister. He enlisted as part of the 203rd Battalion's medical personnel (unclear from MÍH whether he was a medic or stretcher bearer) and continued to serve in a medical capacity when transferred to the 8th Battalion. He is described in MÍH as intelligent and a good speaker.

MÍH states that he had participated in (and survived) fighting in Bourbon Forest before falling at Cambrai, but that his parents never received a clear explanation as to why he was reported as missing but later dead. He is described as strong and intelligent, talented and steadfast, with a love of learning and books. He was of somewhat larger than average build, with fair hair, a high and prominent forehead, blue eyes and an intelligent expression.

event.p: Enlisted in 1916.

Embarked with his regiment for England in March or May 1917 (MÍH: 7 May 1917 is probably correct; his service records give the date 3 March but this seems to be an error as he is listed as arriving in England on 14 May 1917), where he was trained as a sniper. According to MÍH, he was so good a sniper that he was offered a position as shooting instructor but turned this down and went instead to France in October 1917, where he joined the Machine Gunners.

On 7 November 1917 (MÍH: 6 November), he received a near-fatal headwound (gunshot wound to the left side of the head) during an attack on the German trenches at Ypres in Belgium. His company had already seized two trenches, before he was wounded at 5 a.m. in the morning; his company took an additional two trenches in this action. He was unconscious for 10 days and not expected to live, but he came to and was in reasonably good health when he returned home in July 1918. He was medically discharged on 15 July 1918.

Died at King George's Hospital in Winnipeg. He fell ill on 14 March 1919 and was 10 days in hospital before his death. Given the description of his health on discharge (at which point he suffered from constant headache, dizziness and pain in his head, in addition to deafness and ringing in his left ear), his war injury was almost certainly a major contributing factor in his death.

He refused to work in this capacity as he had enlisted in the army to fight, not hold a desk job (MÍH: "Kvaðst hafa í herinn gengið til að berjast, en eigi til að sitja við bókfærslu."). In order to reach the front, he reverted to the rank of private and went to France in February 1915.
Fatally wounded by a shell and died soon after.

According to Minningarrit íslenskra hermanna, he was hit during a massive attack on the Canadians' front-line trenches and died while the field ambulence was attending to his wounds. He was concious and shortly before death asked those present to give his love to his family ("Var með rænu og bað að skila kveðju sinni heim, en dó svo skömmu síðar.").

A second copy of the attestation paper, marked as a duplicate, has his birth year (1899) "corrected" to 1897.

According to MÍH, he was the victim of a gas attack in the trenches, some time between May and August 1917 (but probably at Hill 70 in August 1917 when he was also wounded). The gas attack is not mentioned in his service records, but according to MÍH

According to MÍH, he was seriously wounded in fighting at Hill 70. He was treated at field hospital, being wounded on 15 August 1917, and admitted to hospital on 19 August 1917 with a gunshot wound to his left arm. He was discharged from hospital on 18 January 1918. He was deemed not fit for service and returned to Canada in March 1918, where he was discharged as medically unfit on 20 August 1918 in Winnipeg due to impaired function of his left arm and forearm. The wound initially healed, but his arm was seriously damaged and in connection with the gas attack was ultimately the cause of his death according to MÍH, as physical exertion on return to civilian life exacerbated his injuries.

Died at Winnipeg General Hospital. According to MÍH, he had returned to Winnipeg for an operation to his arm in the fall of 1920 and never regained his health after the operation, dying after enduring great suffering.

Helgason of Dafoe, Saskatchewan. According to MÍH, he left Winnipeg with his regiment on 12 September 1916 and the next summer went to France, where he participated in several battles. According to his service records, he was transferred to the 16th Battalion and was 3 1/2 months in France; he was decorated with "one gold bar". The Govenment of Canada gave him a homestead, probably in Manitoba somewhere north of Winnipeg, but physical exertion exacerbated his condition and he was hospitalized in 1920. He is described as somewhat taller than average, thin and mannerly, light-haired, blue-eyed and personable and the best of men. event.p: Enlisted in March 1916. The witness on his attestation paper was A.J. Polson (Archibald Jón Polson).
Killed in action at Vimy Ridge.

person.note: Regimental number 722232. His parents were Pálína Guðbjörg Stefánsdóttir (daughter of Stefán Jónasson from Þverá in Blönduhlíð and Guðbjörg Tómasdóttir from Nautabúi in Blönduhlíð, Iceland) and Stefán Eiríksson (son of Lilja Guðnadóttir and Eiríkur Eiríksson from Djúpidalur in Akrahreppur in Skagafjarðarsýsla, Iceland), who farmed at Nýjabær, near Gimli, in New Iceland. They emigrated in 1888 and lived in Gimli from that time. Júlíus lived with his parents at the time he enlisted in the army. According to MÍH, he left Winnipeg with his regiment on 12 September, but the date on which he arrived from England to France was unknown; he was in France by early in 1917. He was in the trenches until he fell at the Battle of Vimy Ridge. He had a brother, police officer Valdimar Stefánsson of Gimli, and an older half-brother, Stefán Eldjárnsson, who was a farmer in the Gimli area. Júlíus is described as a handsome boy, very intelligent, which was a trait inherited from both sides of his family. ("Júlíus var mesti myndarpiltur, vel greindur, sem hann átti kyn til í báðar ættir.")

person.affiliation: 243rd Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, 5th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Saskatchewan Regiment)

event.p: Enlisted in January 1917.
Embarked with his regiment for England on 28 May 1917 on the SS Olympic. He arrived in France on 1 September 1917 and joined his unit on 6 October.
Fatally wounded on 10 November 1917, after just over a month on the front.
Died of his wounds at No. 2 Casualty Clearing Station.

person.note: Regimental number 1051441. His parents were Jón Halldórsson (from Hrauntún in Þingvallasveit, Árnessýsla, Iceland) and Guðrún Sigríður Kaprasíusdóttir (from Reykjavík) of Sinclair in Pipestone, Manitoba, Canada. They emigrated in 1886 and spent several years at Argyle before moving to Sinclair in 1899. Konráð was the youngest of 8 siblings, of whom only 3 were still alive when MÍH was published. Konráð began working at a young age, first at an ironmongery or hardware store (járnvöruverslun) and later as a tinsmith. He worked as a tinsmith in Brock, Saskatchewan, from the spring of 1916 until he enlisted in 1917. He is described as handsome, with light reddish-brown hair and blue eyes. He was popular among his peers, for he was the best of boys in word and deed. ("Hann var vinsæll af jafnöldrum sínum, enda hinn bezti drengur í orði og verki.")

person.birth: 17 August 1888 at Hóll in Kaldakinn in Suður-Þingeyjarsýsla, Iceland.

event.p: Kristín began her nursing career in 1916, but it is unclear whether she formally joined the Canadian Army Medical Corp in November-December 1917 or October 1918.
Contracted Spanish Flu while working on the isolation ward for soldiers who had contracted the disease (MÍH).
Died in hospital in Edmonton a few days after falling ill.

person.note: Her parents were Guðlaug Sesselja Pétursdóttir from Miklahóll in Viðvíkursveit, Skagafjarðarsýsla, Iceland, and Friðrik Friðriksson, also of Skagafjörður. They lived at Glenboro in Manitoba, where Kristín was buried in the Brú Cemetery. Kristín studied nursing at Strathcona Hospital (today the University of Alberta Hospital) in Edmonton. She completed her degree and graduated on 16 March 1916, achieving the highest grade. From graduation until 1 November 1917, she lived with her parents in Glenboro, Manitoba, before accepting a position at Strathcona Hospital and enlisting in the Canadian Army Medical Corp, where she attended with great care to patients from the Canadian Army. Her work on the isolation ward was not without danger, and she herself became a victim of the epidemic.

event.p: Enlisted in November 1916 in Moose Jaw.
Embarked with his regiment for England on 16 April.
Received a wound to the face and arm in November 1917 but was able to rejoin his unit in February 1918 despite the severity of the wounds.
Fatally wounded on 2 September, with a gunshot wound to his right leg and a fractured shoulder.

Died of his wounds at Casualty Clearing Station No. 33. The family believed that he had died on 12 September after being wounded on 2 September, but he is listed in official records as having died the same day. The family had no knowledge of his whereabouts at the time, but believed that he had died at or near Ypres, as they had heard the 5th battalion might have been there at the time. He was, however, buried in Ligny-St.Flochel British Cemetery in France.

person.note: Regimental number 268064. His parents were Jón Jónsson (a hreppstjóri or parish administrative officer, d. 1902) and his second wife Málfríður Kristín Jósefsdóttir. Magnús's mother lived with her son Guðmundur in Stykkishólmur, Iceland, at the time of MÍH's publication, but at least one brother (Gunnl. J. Johnson) seems to have lived in Winnipeg. According to MÍH, Magnús lived at Mouse River in North Dakota, USA, where worked as a farm labourer, but enlisted in Moose Jaw; he resided in Moose Jaw according to his attestation paper, but this is uncertain since the United States had not yet entered the war and Magnús could not thus have given Mouse River as his place of residence. He may also have been a migratory worker. According to MÍH, he embarked for England in April 1916 (a typo for 1917) and went to France after additional training in England. He is mentioned as having written letters home.

person.birth: 21 October 1892 in Selkirk, Manitoba, Canada.
person.education: According to MÍH, Magnús enrolled in the University of Manitoba and graduated in 1915 with a degree in history and economics. After this, he went to Morse, Saskatchewan, to his brother-in-law, Buhr, who was a lawyer, and was learning to practice law with him.

event.p: Enlisted in April 1916.

Killed in air combat, according to MÍH when a British flyer ran into his aircraft by accident. Both pilots were killed.

person.note: His parents were Þorsteinn Þorkelsson Kelly (born in Iceland at Unastaðir in Hjaltadalur in Skagafjarðarsýsla, son of Þorkell Guðmundsson and Hallfríður) and Guðrún Björnsdóttir (daughter of Björn Guðmundsson and his first wife Sigríður Bjarnadóttir, who lived at Reynistaðarhreppur in Skagafjarðarsýsla; Sigríður was of the Sjávarborgarætt family). Magnús's parents lived first at Steinárgerði in Svartárdalur in Húnaþing and later at Leifsstaðir. They emigrated to North America in 1883, living first at Arnes in New Iceland (Árnesbyggð) but from 1891 in Selkirk. Magnús's father, Þorsteinn, died in Selkirk on 20 May 1897. His son Björn inherited the family home, and Guðrún lived with him. He had three sisters: Guðrún Búason (d. 1921), Sigríður Hill (married, in Winnipeg) and María Buhr (married, in Morse). He married Florence Kelly in 1916, between April and November. They lived at Portage la Prairie in November 1916, but she later moved to Lion's Head, Ontario. According to MÍH, he was an accomplished athlete, having won many medals ("30-10 verðlaunapeninga") at sporting events before graduating. On arrival to England, he trained as a fighter pilot, evidently completing his training in April 1918.

person.birth: 2 June 1893 (or possibly 19 June 1894) at Foam Lake, Saskatchewan, Canada.
person.death: Missing and presumed killed in action 30-31 October 1917.
person.affiliation: 68th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Regina), Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry

event.p: Enlisted in 1915.

Embarked with his regiment for England on 1 May 1916 (MÍH: 21 April). Fought at Vimy Ridge, the Somme and Ypres. Twice in 1917 he was one of the few survivors of an offensive of the Princess Patricias.
Survived a gas attack in September 1916

Reported missing in action on 30-31 October 1917, in an offensive under heavy shelling at the Battle of Passchendaele. It was one of the heaviest days of fighting in which his regiment participated, with very few survivors. Magnús was not found among the wounded or survivors and presumed dead.

person.note: Regimental number 105590. His parents were Stefán Ólafsson from Skeiðahreppur in Árnessýsla and Guðrún Hinriksdóttir from Seltjarnarnes (sister of Magnús Hinriksson in Churchbridge, SK). They moved from Iceland to the Thingvalla settlement in Saskatchewan (Þingvallabyggð) but moved to Foam Lake in 1892 or 1893, where Magnús became one of the first Icelandic children born in the settlement. Guðrún passed away at Foam Lake, but Magnús's father continued to live in the area with his daughter and son-in-law Jón Þórðarson Vium from Valshamar in Geiradalur. According to MÍH, he sent home a knife or dagger (tygilhnífur) and the insignia from his hat, which had been shot in two.

person.note: Regimental number 186668. Bjarni Þórarinsson of Reykjavík. According to MÍH, Magnús left for England in the summer of 1916 and that same fall departed for France. He was on the battlefield almost constantly until he fell in March 1917. Magnús is described as artistic and intelligent. He was energetic, progressive, self-assertive and determined, good-hearted and generous, and ("Hann var hinn röskasti, framsækinn og fylginn sér og ótrauður, góðhjartaður og drenglyndur, og mátti það í mörgu merkja, þótt ungur væri.")

Stefán settled at Víðivellir in Arnes, Manitoba, Canada. Although he was not married at the time he signed his attestation paper, Magnús married Guttormína Kristín Brynjólfsdóttir Anderson prior to leaving Canada. She lived in Winnipeg at the time of the publication of MÍH. According to MÍH, Magnús embarked for England on 7 April 1917 and from there went to France.

person.note: Regimental number 294902. His parents were Jón Metúsalemsson (John Mathews) from Möðrudal á Fjöllum and Stefanía Stefánsdóttir from Stakkahlíð in Loðmundarfjörður. Methúsalem grew up with his parents, living at the Álftavatnsbyggð Settlement and later Siglunesbyggð Settlement in Manitoba, Canada. After his father's death in 1915, he assumed responsibility for the household. He farmed and fished to support the family before enlisting. He arrived on the front lines before Christmas of 1917 and remained in the trenches until he fell in battle. He is described as a man of average height, (svaraði sér vel, well-proportioned, well-built, responsive?), quick and lively in conversation, a spirited man and (öruggur til allra framkvæmda). Always ready to help, whenever someone was in a tight spot, and this made him popular. ("Metúsalem var meðalmaður á hæð og svaraði sér vel, snar og fjörugur í máli, gleðimaður og öruggur til allra framkvæmda. Reiðubúinn til að hjálpa, hvenær sem einhver átti í vök að verjast, og aflaði það honum vinsældir.")

person.note: Regimental number 722035. His parents were Guðni Ólason and Margrét Þórðardóttir, who emigrated in 1887 from Gíslastaðir with five of their children and farmed at Akra, ND, USA, for over 20 years. Óli remained in Iceland and was fostered by Einar Jónsson of Stórasandfell, his mother Margrét's foster-brother. Óli grew up at Stórasandfell but at age 25 he married Ólöf Jónsdóttir from Arnkelsgerði á Völlum and the couple left for North America in 1909. In the army, he worked mainly as a driver according to MÍH, leaving for England on 12 September 1916. After he was transferred to the 16th Battalion, he fought as a regular infantryman and participated in all battles with his regiment until he fell. He is described as a strong man, patient in adversity, and the best of men.

His parents lived in Lundar in Manitoba (Lundar í Álftavatnsbyggð), where Guðmundur grew up. He is described as tall, thin and lithe, with light hair, bright eyes and a clear, many expression. He was a handsome man, with an intelligent expression. He was an eager learner, and was determined to pursue his education, had he lived to do so. ("Hann var fríðleiksmaður og bar svipur hans allur vott um ríkt gáfnafar. Hann var mjög námfús og hafði ásett sér, að afla sér fræðslu og þekkingar, ef aldur hefði unnist til.")

Killed in action.

person.note: Regimental number 1001072. His parents were Stefán Jóhannsson from Litli-Ás (or Litli-Ós) in Vatnsnes and Sólveig Ólafsdóttir from Kirkjuvogshafnir in Gullbringusýsla. Óskar was descended from amtmaður Stefán Þórarinsson (b. 1754) and Governor Magnús Stephensen (b. 1836). Óskar and his father enlisted on the same day in the same battalion; they were quickly transferred to the 223rd Battalion, and left Winnipeg for England on 7 April 1917. His father, Stefán, worked on railway construction for the Canadian army and was made a corporal; he survived the war (MÍH p. 159). In mid-November in 1917, Óskar was sent to the front. He remained in the trenches until his death. Óskar is described as promising looking, well built and handsome, with beautiful eyes, light hair and a broad, high forehead. He was the most promising of youths. ("Hann var gerfilegur piltur í sjón, fallega vaxinn og fríður sýnum, fagureygður, bjartur á hár og ennið hátt og mikið. Hann var hið efnilegasta ungmenni.")

His father passed away in or before 1890 and his widowed mother worked as a servant in 1890; Páll was probably a pauper in Austur-Skaftafellssýsla after his father's death and raised by a foster family (although not mentioned in MÍH). According to MÍH, he emigrated to Winnipeg in 1910 and lived there for six years. His address of "Big Island" could refer to a lake in Northern Manitoba or (as is likely) a translation of "Mikley" ('Big Island'), i.e., Hecla Island. He is described as a very active man, tall and bulky, strong and manly, with a benign air that nevertheless spoke to his tenacity and strength of mind. He had a fair complexion and grey eyes, introverted by nature and not a man of many words, a fast friend and loyal to his family.

person.note: Regimental number 722230. Pétur was married to Jónína Hrólfsdóttir, and they had three children. At the time of MÍH's publication, Jónína and her children lived in Gimli. According to MÍH, he embarked with his regiment for England on 12 September 1916 and to France on 20 February. He fought in various battles in the spring and summer of 1917 before being wounded on 8 November; he recovered in hospital and returned to the front in January 1918. He obtained 10 days' leave at the beginning of August and visited England. He returned on 11 August and fell in battle five days later. He is described as a large man with a dark complexion, brisk and energetic. Good-natured and willing to help others to the best of his abilities, especially those less fortunate than he. ("Pétur var stór maður vexti, dökkur yfirlitum og hinn karlmannlegasti, röskur að verki og orkumikill. Góðlyndur og hjálpfús eftir því sem ástæður leyfðu, einkum við þá, er minni voru máttar.")

He was hit with shrapnel; his right leg was shattered below the knee, his right shoulder, neck and left thigh were hit, and a large piece of metal shrapnel lodged in his chest. His condition stabilized, and he was sent to hospital in England, where the shattered right leg was amputated on 3 June 1917 and his wounds healed partially. He was sent to Canada in December 1917, arriving on 9 January 1918. He received further treatment in hospital in Canada.

He wrote his mother that he would soon be well again, but the illness dragged on and worsened and was the cause of his death. He was buried in England. He is described as a particularly promising boy, handsome and cheerful, and thus popular with his peers. He was sensitive and good-hearted, as shown in his treatment of others, both older and younger. ("Sigurjón var einkar efnilegur piltur, friður sýnum og glaðlyndur. Stefán and Sigríður moved to Reykjavík in 1881, where Stefán worked as a stonemason. They emigrated to Canada in 1887, where Stefán changed his name to Stephan Thorson; they lived in Winnipeg until 1913, when Stephan was elected mayor of Gimli. Stephan's parents moved to the West Coast in 1922. Both his parents are described as intelligent, and his father in particular was deeply involved in the Icelandic community in Winnipeg. Three brothers were alive and living in Winnipeg at the time of MÍH's publication: Jón, a railway mail clerk; Joseph Thorarinn Thorson, a lawyer and dean of the School of Law at the University of Manitoba (and later a Member of Parliament); and the artist Carl (Charlie) Thorson. Stephan Helgi survived the battles at Ypres and the Somme without being wounded, before being killed in action. He is described as a particularly intelligent boy, sharp-witted and hotheaded, competitive and self-assertive. He was of average height, rather slim and dark-haired and -complexioned. ("Stephan Helgi var einkar vel gefinn piltur, bráðskýr og örgerður í lund, kappsamur og fylginn sér. Hann var meðal maður á vexti, fremur grannur og dökkur á brún og brá.")

The family settled near Arborg. According to MÍH, Sveinn left Winnipeg with his regiment on 7 April 1917 for England and was in the trenches in France in December that winter. He was in the trenches from December until he fell. He is described in MÍH as a handsome boy and strong and tough, even though he was under twenty when he died. ("myndarpiltur hinn mesti og vaskleikamaður orðinn, þótt eigi væri hann nema tæplega tvítugur.")

person.birth: 31 January 1881 at Björnólfsstaðir in Langidalur, Húnavatnssýsla, Iceland

event.p: Enlisted in 1915.
Embarked with his regiment for England on 31 October 1916. Shortly after his arrival, he went to France.
Minor injuries; according to MÍH, he was slightly wounded on 13 December 1917 and spent several days in hospital. He was immediately sent back to the trenches after recovery.
Killed by a shell. According to MÍH, his army chaplain wrote to the family and reported that he had been bringing supplies for his fellow soldiers at the time.

person.note: Regimental number . His parents were Jónas Jónsson and Margrét Jónsdóttir (d. 1888).He was survived by his elderly father, a brother Jón in Akra and a half-sister Sigríður Hjaltdal in St. James, MB.

event.p: Enlisted in 1915.
Embarked with his regiment for England in the summer of 1915 (no exact date given). Went to the front soon after and fought at the Somme, Sanctuary Woods and Vimy Ridge.
Fatally wounded in fighting at Tilloy (near Cambrai).
Died of his wounds.

person.note: His parents were Ólafur Loftsson (Oliver Loptson) from Hlíðarendi in Flókadalur in Borgarfjarðarsýsla (a goldsmith) and his wife Guðrún. His siblings were: the Rev. Aðalsteinn Magnús (missionary in "Wu-Chow, Kwang-Tei" in China), Loftur Páll in Winnipeg and Anna (a trained nursing professional, who worked in Alberta, "heilbrigðisumsjónarkona við alþýðuskóla í Alberta-fylkis").

person.affiliation: 108th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Selkirk), 16th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Manitoba Regiment)

event.p: Enlisted in February 1916.
Embarked with his regiment for England on 18 September 1916 and from there went to France in February 1917.
Severely wounded on 10 April 1917. Received a shell or gunshot wound to his left thigh. He was in hospital until November 1917, but returned to the front in May 1918.
Again wounded on 17 August 1918, with a gunshot wound to the neck. He was hospitalized but discharged in September 1918.
Reported wounded and missing on 1 October 1918 at the Somme.

person.note: Regimental number 722091. His parents were Páll Jóhannesson and Þórlaug Einarsdóttir from Mjóifjörður in Iceland. They moved to Canada in 1883 and settled at Icelandic River (Riverton). Sveinbjörn was married to Guðrún Ísleifsdóttir (daughter of Ísleifur Sigurgeirsson from Barkarstaðir in Fljótshlíð in Rangárvallasýslu, Iceland). The couple lived at Arborg in Manitoba. He is described as strong and a hard worker. ("Sveinbjörn var þrekmaður mikill og dugnaðarmaður.").

person.birth: 21 May 1901 in Bakki, Tjörnes, Suður-Þingeyjarsýsla, Iceland.

event.p: Emigrated in 1912 with his family.

person.affiliation: 223rd Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Canadian Scandinavians), 27th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (City of Winnipeg)

event.p: Enlisted in March 1917 in Winnipeg, when he was 15.
Embarked with his regiment for England on 3 May 1917. He arrived on the front line in France in December 1917.
Killed in fighting at Arras.

person.note: Regimental number 294900. His parents were Andrés Þorbergsson from Syðri-Tunga in Tjörnes and Aðalbjörg Pálína Guðmundsdóttir from Húsavík við Skjálfanda, Suður-Þingeyjarsýsla, Iceland. They were living at Icelandic River (Riverton) at the time of MÍH's publication. According to MÍH, Þorbergur worked on the railway at the time he enlisted in March 1917. Þorbergur was probably the youngest Icelandic-born soldier to fall in the First World War (the only born in 1901). According to MÍH, he fought at Passchendaele, Amiens and Arras. He is described in MÍH as having been praised as selfless and never one to shrink from that which was asked of him (?); he was always among the first to volunteer for a dangerous assignment. ("Honum var sá vitnisburður borinn, að hann hefði verið sérlega ósérhlífinn og ógjarn á að teljast undan því, sem krafist var. Var hann ætíð með þeim fyrstu til að bjóða sig fram, er til einhverra mannrauna kom og leitað var til sjálfboða til þeirra hluta.")

person.birth: 1 May 1876 at Bakkagerði in Stöðvarfjörður, Suður-Múlasýsla, Iceland.

event.p: Emigrated in 1905, with a group of 10 relatives, and settled in Winnipeg.

person.affiliation: 108th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Selkirk), 16th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Manitoba Regiment)

event.p: Enlisted in 1916.
Wounded in action at Hill 70. Fatal gunshot wounds. According to MÍH, the hospital chaplain reported that he had been shot in both hips and his left arm, and that his wounds were untreatable.
Died at Casualty Clearing Station No. 33.

person.note: Regimental number 721867. His parents were Björn Jónsson and Lukka Stefánsdóttir of Bakkagerði in Stöðvarfjörður. According to MÍH, he sailed for England on 13 September 1916 and was sent to the front in the spring of 1917. He was an especially gentle-natured man, peaceful and private, loyal and a fast friend. He was of average height, rather small-featured, blue-eyed and blonde-haired. He was the best of men and universally esteemed among those who knew him. ("Þórarinn var sérstaklega lundþýður maður, friðgjarn og fáskiftinn, tryggur og vinfastur. Hann var meðalmaður vexti, fremur smáleitur, bláeygður og ljósgulur á hár. Hann var hinn bezti drengur og hvarvetna vel metinn á meðal þeirra er honum kyntust.")

person.birth: 19 April 1894 (MÍH: the first day of summer, i.e., in the traditional Icelandic calendar) in Cavalier, North Dakota, USA.
person.affiliation: 1st Depot Battalion, Saskatchewan Regiment

event.p: Drafted in January 1918.
Contracted pneumonia shortly after arriving at training camp and was invalided home in March of 1917, where he spent the summer.
Returned to training camp on 12 October 1918 and contracted the Spanish Flu very shortly after arrival.
According to MÍH, his father came to the camp and brought him home, but he continued to worsen in spite of treatment. He died on 21 October 1918 at home.

person.note: Regimental number 256890. His parents were Sigurjón Eyríksson and Kristrún Þorkelsdóttir of Wynyard, Saskatchewan, Canada. They moved to Wynyard in 1907. His paternal grantparents (Sigurjón's father Eiríkur and mother Halldóra Sigurðardóttir) were from Gilhagi in Goðdalasókn in Skagafjörður. His maternal grandparents (Kristrún's father Þorkell Bessason from Gil in Jökuldalur and mother Þorbjörg Sveinsdóttir from Hafrafell in Fell in Norður-Múlasýsla) emigrated in 1876, when Kristrún was a little girl. Þorkell and the editor Jón Ólafsson were second cousins: Þorbjörg Sveinsdóttir's father was the brother of Jón Ólafsson's grandfather. Þorkell is described as a very promising man, tall and strong, tender-hearted and even-tempered and wanted only amicable relations with others (?). ("efnismaður hinn mesti, mikill vexti og hraustmenni, geðljúfur og jafnlyndur og vildi eigi öðru en góðu skipta við alla.")

person.birth: 1890 or 10 July 1895 in Muskoka, Ontario, Canada.
person.affiliation: 122nd Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Muskoka), Canadian Forestry Corps (53rd Company)

event.p: Enlisted in March 1916.
Embarked with his regiment for England on 28 May 1917.
Injured and admitted to hospital at Rouen on 23 October 1917. Rejoined his unit in December 1917.
Fell severely ill on 22 July 1918 while on leave in Scotland.
Died at 3rd Scottish General Hospital in Glasgow (cause of death: pneumonia following influenza).

person.note: Regimental number 763404. His parents were Ágúst Guðmundsson Goodman from Akureyri and his wife Emily Jane, of Rosseau, Ontario. According to MÍH, the Goodmans had three sons, all of whom were in the army. Thomas Goodman is buried in Glasgow, Scotland.

person.birth: 12 May 1894 at Nýlenda in Leira in Gullbringusýsla, Iceland.

event.p: Emigrated with his family in 1900, when he was 6.

person.affiliation: 223rd Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Canadian Scandinavians), Canadian Engineers (1st Battalion of the Canadian Engineers)

event.p: Enlisted in August 1916.
Embarked with his regiment for England on 3 May 1917 on the SS Justicia (MÍH: 7 April).
Promoted to corporal on 1 November 1917.

Contracted Spanish Flu in March 1919. He was hospitalized in France, then sent to England. According to MÍH, he was scarcely able to travel when sent back to Canada, where he was immediately admitted to King Edward Hospital on arrival in Winnipeg, where he remained until his death with the exception of two weeks spent with his parents.
Died in King Edward Hospital in Winnipeg.

person.note: Regimental number 294668. His parents were Hreinn Hreinsson (b. 11 January 1863 at Sperðill in Vestur-Landeyjar, Rangárþing, Iceland, son of Hreinn Guðlaugsson) and Sigríður Þórðardóttir (b. 13 July 1858) from Hlöðutún in Stafholtstungur, Mýrasýsla. They settled at Piney, Manitoba, where Thorsteinn grew up.

person.birth: 27 May 1896 at Urriðaá in Álftaneshreppur, Mýrasýsla, Iceland.

event.p: Emigrated with his older brother Bjarni and parents from Urriðaá in 1897, around or shortly after his first birthday.

person.affiliation: 181st Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Brandon), 16th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (C company)

event.p: Enlisted in March 1916, as did his brother Helgi Thorvaldsson.
Fatally wounded on 6 August 1918 (MÍH).
Died in hospital in France.

person.note: Regimental number 722138. His parents were Jón Þorvaldsson from Urriðaá and Sólveig Bjarnadóttir from Arnarstapi in Álftaneshreppur, Mýrasýsla, Iceland. No picture of Þorvaldur is printed in MÍH; possibly none survives. According to MÍH, he attended public school until his father's death on 2 June 1907, which forced him to quit school and begin working to support his mother and younger siblings. According to MÍH, he left Manitoba on 12 April 1917 and sailed for England with his regiment on 18 April. Both he and his brother Helgi were transferred to the 16th Battalion on arrival in France, and Þorvaldur participated in all battles in which his battalion fought until he was fatally wounded. He is described as a man of great substance, of a good temperament, and loved and admired by all those who knew him. ("Hann var hið bezta mannsefni, lundgóður og hvers manns hugljúfi, er honum kyntist.")

event.p: Enlisted in 1914. According to Minningarrit Íslenskra hermanna, he was one of the first volunteers from Winnipeg and enlisted in the 34th Fort Garry Horse in August 1914, transferring to more than one regiment during the course of the war.

Embarked for Europe on 23 October 1915. He fought in most battles in which the Canadian Army participated. In the summer of 1918, he was offered the choice between promotion to lieutenant or the opportunity to return home in October 1918. He chose the latter but was killed in action in September.
Killed in action in France, 6 September 1918.

person.note: His parents were Guðlaugur Ólafsson from Hagi in Húnaþing and Áslaug Hansdóttir from Þóreyjarnúpur. Minningarrit Íslenskra hermanna mentions that he regularly sent letters home to his parents and family.

person.birth: 19 May 1891 in the Quill Lakes Settlement (Þingvallabyggð) near Churchbridge, Saskatchewan, Canada

person.affiliation: Lord Strathcona's Horse (Royal Canadians), R.C.A.C.

event.p: Enlisted in the Lord Strathcona's Horse in the autumn of 1914.
Embarked for Europe with his regiment on 3 October 1915. He fought at: "Heisseims, Dichbach, Simal, Somme, Peronne, Tevin-Court, Gusen-Court, Bethen-Court, Vaten-Court" (MÍH).

Killed on 27 May 1917 at Vadencourt (Vaten-Court). According to Minningarrit íslenskra hermanna, he was killed when taking two prisoners in a German trench. One of the German soldiers shot him and he died instantly.

person.note: His parents were Jón Þórðarson from Akranes in Borgarfjarðarsýsla (emigrated 1886) and Guðfinna Tómasdóttir from Litla-Ármót í Flóa. They married in Þingvallabyggð and moved with their family to Langruth in 1894.

person.birth: 13 October 1892 in Brandon, Manitoba, Canada.
person.affiliation: 5th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Saskatchewan Regiment)

event.p: Enlisted in the 12th Manitoba Dragoons in August 1914, according to MÍH.
Embarked for England on 3 October 1914.
Seriously injured at St. Julien on 24 April 1916 (MÍH: 27 April). Was offered discharge but refused and was placed again on the front as a sniper.
Killed in action on 26 September 1916. According to MÍH, he had been recommended for a medal for his bravery shortly before his death.

person.note: Regimental number 12772. His parents were Þorleifur Þorvaldsson from Miðhús í Gufudalssveit and Málmfríður Guðlaug Jensdóttir from Skutulsfjörður við Ísafjarðardjúp. According to MÍH, they still lived in Brandon in 1921. Thorvaldur participated in fighting at Ypres, St. Julien and the Somme. He is described as the most promising of men and a great adventurer. (MÍH: "Hinn gervilegasti maður og fullhugi að sama skapi.")

person.birth: 2 July 1896 at White Sand, Saskatchewan, Canada.
person.affiliation: 188th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Saskatchewan), 46th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (South Saskatchewan)

event.p: Enlisted in December 1915.
Embarked with his regiment for England on 12 October 1916, after training in Yorkton and Camp Hughes.
According to MÍH, Thorsteinn was wounded and spent around three weeks in hospital, but recovered and went back to the front.
Killed in action at Vimy Ridge, in the second of two major engagements in which he participated.

person.note: Regimental number 887383. His parents were Þorsteinn Thorsteinsson (born at Holt in Einholtssókn in Hornafjörður, Austur-Skaftafellssýsla) and Anna Jónsdóttir from Ásgrímsstaðir in Hjaltastaðarþinghá in Norður-Múlasýsla. They moved to Canada in the summer of 1891 and spent some time at the Thingvalla settlement (Þingvallabyggð) but moved to Foam Lake in 1898, near the town of Leslie, and have lived there since. There was at one time an Icelandic settlement near White Sand, close to present-day Theodore. MÍH: Thorsteinn was larger than average, with a fair complexion, blue-eyed and promising in his appearance and energy. He was rather reserved and careful with his words, but loyal by nature. His life was not eventful: it might be said that the army was his first adventure, and proved a big one. He joined the army as a volunteer, ready to take what came, be it injury or death; it suited his temperament. He did not criticize others' business and drew little attention to himself. He was conscientious and the best of men. ("Þorsteinn var meira en meðalmaður að vexti, bjartur yfirlitum, bláeygður og hinn gervilegastur að sýn og orku. Fremur var hann fálátur og orðvar, en tryggur í lund. Æfiferill hans var ekki viðburðaríkur: má segja, að hergangan væri fyrsta æfintýrið, enda reyndist það líka stórt. Hann gekk sem sjálfboði í herinn, albúinn að taka því sem verða vildi, sárum eða bana; fór það og að skaplyndi hans. Hann var óádeilinn um annarra sakir og lét ekki mikið yfir sér. Hann var hinn samvizkusamasti í öllu og hinn bezti drengur.")

person.birth: 4 February 1893 in Gimli, Manitoba, Canada.
person.affiliation: Not specified in MÍH

event.p: Drafted in September 1917.
Killed in action in fighting at Hill 225 near Gesnes in France.

person.note: His parents were Sveinbjörn Soffoníasson, born at Grund and raised at Bakki in Vallnahreppur in Eyjafjörður, Iceland, and Snjólaug Runólfsdóttir from Hreiðarstaðir in Vallnahreppur. According to MÍH, he sailed for France on 5 July 1918 and fought at the Battle of Argonne Forest. His parents and siblings lived in Blaine at the time of MÍH's publication.

person.birth: 12 November 1896 in Glenboro, Manitoba, Canada.
person.affiliation: 184th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, 8th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (90th Winnipeg Rifles)

event.p: Enlisted in 1916.
Embarked with his regiment for England in October 1916 (MÍH).
Sickened in May 1917 (MÍH: Trench Fever after six months in the trenches) and was sent to England to recover, returning to the front and fully recovered by March 1918.
Received a fatal shrapnel wound to the head on 13 August 1918.
Died of his wounds at No. 5 Casualty Clearing Station.

person.note: Regimental number 874307. His parents were Ívar Björnsson (b. 21 September 1866) from Skjaldakot in Vatnsleysuströnd and Anna Jónína Valtýsdóttir (b. 1 June 1868) from Húsavík in Borgarfjörður austur. The family moved to Langruth (or Big Point) when Valdimar was 8 years old. His siblings were: Björn, Sigurður, Halldóra, Margrét and Addie Viola of Langruth, MB. According to MÍH, Valdimar was a strong man, nearly 6 feet tall, and burly for his age. He had light hair and a fair complexion and was lively and quick in his movements. He was brave and progressive, popular and esteemed by both superiors and subordinates. ("Valdimar var hraustmenni mikið, þrjár álnir á hæð og þrekinn eftir aldri. Hann var ljós á hár, bjartur yfirlitum, fjörlegur og hvatur í hreyfingum. Hann var djarfur og framsækinn, vinsæll og í áliti meðal æðri sem lægri.")

person.birth: 5 April 1892 in Victoria, BC, Canada.
person.affiliation: Cadet corps (3 years), 67th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Western Scots)

event.p: Enlisted in 1915.
Embarked with his regiment for England on 1 April 1916 (MÍH and one personnel record: 21 April).
Hospitalized after arrival in England in April 1916. Discharged in August and joined his unit that month and fought at Ypres and the Somme.
Fell ill while in the trenches. Hospitalized again in October 1916. Briefly discharged in December and was again in military hospital to May 1917.
Diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and sent to Canada for treatment.
Died at Mountain Sanatorium in Hamilton, Ontario. His body was returned to Victoria, BC, where he was given a military funeral.

person.note: Regimental number 103259. His parents were Steingrímur (Stephen) Norman of Húnavatnssýsla and Lassaríana (Elizabeth) Bjarnadóttir of Mýrasýsla, Iceland.

person.birth: 6 November 1890 near Cavalier, North Dakota, USA.
person.affiliation: 222nd Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, 46th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (South Saskatchewan)

event.p: Enlisted in February 1916.
Killed in action at Passchendaele.

person.note: Regimental number 291563. His parents were Phil O'Dell (born in New York State, USA, of Irish descent) and Ingiríður Ólafsdóttir from Eystrihóll í Fljótum in Skagafjarðarsýsla, Iceland. According to MÍH, he had farmed near Glenboro in Manitoba prior to enlisting; his mother lived in Baldur, Manitoba, at the time of MÍH's publication. According to MÍH, he departed for England on 1 November 1916 and participated in the battles at Vimy Ridge and Hill 70.

person.birth: 8 January 1980 in Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada.
person.occupation: Hardware trade, at Miller Morse Hardware Co.
person.affiliation: 1st Canadian Mounted Rifles, 44th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force (Manitoba)

event.p: Enlisted on 23 December 1914 in the 44th Battalion of the Canadian Expeditionary Force.
Embarked with his regiment for England on 18 October 1915. On arrival in France, he transferred to the Canadian Mounted Rifles.
Killed in action at Sanctuary Wood in Belgium, near Ypres, between 2-5 June 1916.

person.note: Regimental number 622142. His parents were Leonard Preece (born in England) and Jakobína Guðlaugsdóttir from Breiðuvík in Snæfellsnessýsla, Iceland, who emigrated in 1887. He is described as a promising man ("hinn mesti efnismaður").
